newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds papers introduced in tobacco trial.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds papers introduced in tobacco trial.

text.p: The plaintiff's attorney in a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co introduced three internal company documents into evidence on Monday to bolster claims that Reynolds manipulated nicotine levels to keep smokers addicted.
The papers were introduced during the third day of testimony by Dr. Allan Feingold, a Miami physician called by lawyers for Dana Raulerson, who sued Reynolds on behalf of her late sister Jean Connor.
Connor died of lung cancer in October 1995 at age 49.

Raulerson's attorney, Norwood "Woody" Wilner, introduced the documents, written by Reynolds' researcher Claude Teague between 1969 and 1972, to back Feingold's contention that cigarette companies deliberately manipulated nicotine levels.
Wilner said no Florida jury had ever before seen the documents.
Raulerson's lawsuit alleges that cigarettes are addictive, that R.J. Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, knew it and manipulated nicotine levels to keep smokers hooked.

In one document, dated March 28, 1972, and marked confidential, Teague wrote about the possibility of marketing a new type of cigarette and said there would be "no virtue or logic" in decreasing nicotine levels because smokers would simply switch brands.
"Therefore, in designing any cigarette product, the dominant specification should be nicotine delivery," Teague wrote.
Feingold testified that the document showed that specific levels of nicotine were a design element of cigarettes and said the design had a "lethal consequence."

In a 1969 memo about the design of Salem cigarettes, Teague indicated that the company had explored a reduction of nicotine as a way of creating a "safer" cigarette but concluded that any decrease could damage the industry.

"Thus unless some miraculous solution to the smoking-health problem is found, the present 'safer' cigarette strategy, while prudent and fruitful for the short term, may be equivalent to long-term liquidation of the cigarette industry," the memo said.
The document spoke about how to get "pre-smokers" to try cigarettes and defined "pre-smoker" as a "person, usually young, who has never been a smoker."

In an April 1972 document titled "The Nature of the Tobacco Business and the Crucial Role of Nicotine Therein," Teague wrote: "In a sense, the tobacco industry may be thought of as being a specialized, highly ritualized and stylized segment of the pharmaceutical industry."
"Tobacco products, uniquely, contain and deliver nicotine, a potent drug with a variety of physiological effects."
"Happily for the tobacco industry, nicotine is both habituating and unique in its variety of physiological actions."
The document concluded that the standard cigarette's delivery of 1.3 milligrams of nicotine "appear to satisfy" the typical smoker.
"This, somewhat crudely, established a target dosage level for design of new products," Teague wrote.
Feingold testified that 1.3 milligrams was "a very dangerous level of nicotine ... more than sufficient" to sustain an addiction.
